title: Soloviev
hookLine: a Russian philosopher who longed for the reunion of the churches

lines: A CHARMING RULER. A HARD REFUSAL.
cards: A strange story ends in the wilderness. The world has fallen under a smooth, charming ruler who offers everyone exactly what they want, and the world takes the deal.
The few Christians who refuse him gather outside, with three leaders at their head: an Orthodox elder named John, a pope named Peter, and a Protestant scholar named Pauli. Peter, John and Paul.

Near the story's end, those three churches become one again. The man who wrote that tale was Vladimir Soloviev, a Russian Orthodox philosopher, and the ending wasn't decoration. It was the thing he longed for.

teach.h: A WOUND BETWEEN EAST AND WEST
teach.b: Soloviev was a philosopher and a poet, and much of his thinking circled one wound: the split between the churches of East and West, which this path met earlier. He didn't treat it as a technical problem for committees.
He treated it as a break in a family.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE
teach.b: A prayer of Jesus in John's Gospel, spoken on the night before he died, names the hope he kept circling: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us."
He also wrote about what he called Godmanhood: God and humanity coming together, first in Christ, and then, he hoped, drawing all of humanity into one shared life.
A divided church, to him, was that life torn down the middle. He loved his own Orthodox church, and he also wrote warmly of Rome, and some on both sides were uneasy with him for it.

Christians today hold different hopes for what unity would mean: shared communion, shared leadership, or a deep friendship that leaves real differences standing. His tale doesn't settle that. It does something quieter.

It puts the names of three apostles on three churches and lets them stand side by side in the dark, refusing the same false ruler, recognizing each other at last. Readers still argue over what the scene says about Rome.
But the picture it leaves is a family back together.

how: Christians of different churches pray for unity in their own services, and some gather each year for shared prayer for Christian unity; Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant leaders also meet in ongoing dialogue.

games.q: in Soloviev's tale, a charming ruler offers everyone what they want. the few Christians who refuse him gather in the wilderness. what happens next?
o: they argue over who was right all along.
they split into three separate camps.
the Orthodox elder, the pope and the Protestant scholar become one.
games.why: near the end the three churches are reunited: Peter, John and Paul stand together.

practice: Bring to mind a split you know: two churches, two sides of a family, two friends who stopped talking, maybe you and someone. Hold both sides in view, gently, without picking a winner or trying to solve it.
If you pray, you can pray for that reunion in your own words or with Jesus's line, that they all may be one; if you don't, simply wish both sides well.

wordCard.voice: Soloviev. Vladimir Soloviev, the Russian Orthodox philosopher who longed for the churches of East and West to be one family again.

carryVoice: Your line: all one. A family back together, not a victory for one side. See you next time.
